entries.content:
Just a few weeks before Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman premiered on Broadway on February 10, 1949, President Harry Truman elaborated his “Fair Deal” for the American people in his State of the Union address. “We have rejected the discredited theory that the fortunes of the Nation should be in the hands of a privileged few,” he declared. “We have abandoned the ‘trickledown’ concept of national prosperity. Instead, we believe that our economic system should rest on a democratic foundation and that wealth should be created for the benefit of all.” Among other progressive measures, Truman advocated raising corporate taxes, increasing the minimum wage, providing universal health coverage, expanding civil rights protections, and repealing the year-and-a-half-old Taft-Hartley Act that limited the power of labor unions.

No doubt these proposals—and the need for them—were still ringing in the ears of Salesman’s first audiences at the elegant, 950-seat Morosco Theatre in the heart of Times Square (demolished in 1982 to make way for the looming Marriott Marquis Hotel). Miller recounted in his autobiography, Timebends, that no one clapped when the final curtain came down on the play’s first performances. Some men covered their faces while others wept openly, Miller wrote, and it “seemed forever before someone remembered to applaud.”

It’s easy to see why. Willy Loman’s self-deluded self-sacrifice near the end is heart-wrenching, as are the closing words of his wife, Linda, at his graveside: “I made the last payment on the house today. Today, dear. And there’ll be nobody home. We’re free and clear. We’re free. We’re free. We’re free.” But the state of the country at the beginning of 1949 must also have contributed to the audience’s stunned response. It’s only in retrospect that we can see the play as taking place on the cusp of postwar prosperity, though it is frequently described as unfolding amid that economic boom.

In its own moment, the national mood was grim. Over the preceding year, GDP had been falling and unemployment was on the rise. The same edition of The New York Times in which Brooks Atkinson proclaimed Salesman “superb” carried stories covering a “new plunge” on Wall Street, “nervous trading” in the widely fluctuating grain market, and a decline in consumer spending. Government and media outlets deliberately spoke about “disinflation” and “readjustment” rather than “depression” in order to allay public fears that the nation might backslide into the catastrophe that had abated only a decade earlier. Attacks on Truman’s proposals from the congressional right stressed individualism as America’s animating spirit, a callous ethos very much at the crux of Salesman.

None of these factors is explicitly cited in the play; like the never-named products that Willy sells, the war itself is barely mentioned, though both sons, Biff and Happy, would have been old enough to be drafted. Miller’s dramatic universe was more mythic than meticulously pinpointed. Still, economic precarity suffuses the Lomans’ home like a toxic fog. That haze hangs heavily in our own times—a feeling that is made material in the director Joe Mantello’s revelatory new production, where mist frequently rolls in from the wings.

Certain lines draw rueful laughs, or at least did both times I saw this production. For instance, when Happy complains, “I don’t know what the hell I’m workin’ for. Sometimes I sit in my apartment—all alone. And I think of the rent I’m paying. And it’s crazy.” Or when Willy rails, “Once in my life I would like to own something outright before it’s broken! I’m always in a race with the junkyard!… They time those things. They time them so when you finally paid for them, they’re used up.”

Those moments hint at a deeper sense of recognition. Audiences nowadays share a structure of feeling with those who first saw the play. Even people paying upwards of $800 for the best orchestra seats can’t be oblivious to the pervasive economic anxiety, unstable employment, and dubious social mobility of 2026. One might not think that Salesman could seem truly disturbing after its decades as a staple of high school syllabi; many theatergoers arrive already knowing that it will indict the crushing mendacity of the American Dream. Yet Mantello and his excellent cast, led by Nathan Lane and Laurie Metcalf, turn a CliffsNotes cliché into a fully felt, even shocking demonstration of how hope can curdle into reactionary ressentiment when confronted with the relentless brutality of that empty promise. More than in any of the four (out of five) previous Broadway revivals I have seen, the play lands now with fearsome power.

It has long been something of a canard that Miller was the standard-bearer for midcentury American drama’s kitchen-sink realism. His breakthrough, All My Sons, which opened in 1947, was in fact the last of his works to fully take this form. A domestic story with social overtones, it rehearses a driving conflict in Salesman: a son confronting his father over his moral failing. In this case, the father is a manufacturer who protected his profits by knowingly sending defective engine parts to the US Air Force during World War II, causing the death of American fighter pilots. (A recent London production starring Brian Cranston and Marianne Jean-Baptiste, shown in US cinemas through the National Theatre Live program, amply demonstrated how, in the hands of great actors, even Miller’s most nakedly contrived plotting can pack an emotional wallop.)

As the idea for the new play floated in his imagination, Miller went to see Tennessee Williams’s A Streetcar Named Desire. That production, Miller wrote, opened a creative door for him, giving him “a license to speak at full throat,” and confirming his sense that Salesman “could not be encompassed by conventional realism.” His first notion for staging it, Miller revealed in an introduction to his collected plays, was “an enormous face the height of the proscenium arch which would appear and then open up, and we would see the inside of a man’s head.” (The Inside of His Head was Miller’s draft title.) In Salesman, the sequential causality of standard realism gives way to Willy’s sense that past and present exist simultaneously and indistinguishably—a rejection of the “linear or eventual” method of All My Sons, as Miller wrote, in which each event inexorably leads to the next. The scenic designer Jo Mielziner translated Miller’s concept visually for the premiere production by filling the stage with a two-story house, entirely open in front as if the façade had been sliced away, and the side walls scrim-covered frames that could appear transparent. Characters in the present-tense action came in through doors, but figures from the past crossed the downstage perimeter as they entered Willy’s mind. This design realized Miller’s idea so precisely that Miller wrote it into the stage directions of the published text.

Salesman debuted to ecstatic daily reviews, but over the years that followed critics who wrote for “serious” magazines like Partisan Review and Commentary derided Miller’s melodramatic mechanics. Of a climactic confrontation between Biff and Willy in a Boston hotel room (one of the scenes from the past that floods Willy’s mind), Eleanor Clark chided, “Nothing excuses the triteness and the pseudo-psychoanalytic nature of the Boston scene, dragged in to explain Biff’s failures.” Others lambasted Miller’s dime-store Marxism and, worst of all, his “middlebrow” pretensions—a particularly grave sin in the era when Eric Bentley’s Playwright as Thinker (1946) championed the heady European modernists to American readers, and when a countercultural theatrical movement was beginning to emerge in the US. (The Living Theatre, the experimental pacificist-anarchist troupe, was founded in 1947.) Salesman could hardly have seemed more out of step with these challenges to the commercial theater: Willy Loman came across as “a capitalized Human Being, without being anyone…demanding a statistical attention and generalized, impersonal condolence, like that of the editorial page,” wrote Mary McCarthy.

But as high/low distinctions eroded faster than the Warhol Factory could turn out silkscreens, some of the critics who had judged Miller harshly—Bentley and Robert Brustein, for instance—softened their judgments. After Miller’s death in 2005, Brustein wrote that he had come around to appreciating the “overwhelming power” Miller’s plays had in performance. Bentley was more tepid, but still: “Well, he’s better than I said, probably,” he told an interviewer in 2016. They had to admit that, in his best work, Miller—a carpenter by avocation—builds individual scenes and dramatic arcs with architectural precision. From the opening moments of Salesman, when Willy enters weighed down by his two large sample cases, he begins his downward spiral, and the audience is caught in its gravitational pull.

Like all enduring plays, Salesman has persistently caught its moment in its subsequent major productions—each one rapturously reviewed (and four of them, including Mantello’s, winning Best Revival Tony Awards). The first Broadway revival opened in 1975, when New York was on the brink of fiscal collapse, and by all accounts George C. Scott’s Willy—“like both bull and bullfighter in an arena,” wrote Clive Barnes in The New York Times—railed mightily and collapsed heavily under the weight of forces beyond his control. Nearly a decade later, in the greed-is-good Reagan years, Dustin Hoffman offered a feisty and antic Willy, a man scuttling along the tracks of the zeitgeist, unable to climb aboard the train. When Brian Dennehy took on the role in 1999, the Dow was about to cross 10,000 for the first time and the federal government was running a budget surplus. Amid a mood of economic confidence, Dennehy zeroed in on Willy’s inner drama, drawing deep empathy for a man experiencing excruciating psychological pain.

In 2012 the director Mike Nichols, who had said that seeing the original 1949 production as a teenager ignited his interest in theater, reverently reproduced its look and sound, using Mielziner’s set and Alex North’s flute-forward incidental music; his Willy, Philip Seymour Hoffman, presented a harrowing study of bewildered isolation: slumped, self-loathing, laboring to believe in the go-get-’em platitudes he spouts. Then, four years ago, as the surge of white support for the Black Lives Matter movement was subsiding, Wendell Pierce led a cast of black actors as the Lomans. Other characters were played by white actors, adding a stinging layer of racism to the obstacles Willy faces; Pierce was shattering in his forced buoyancy. More than previous revivals, that production (which originated at London’s Young Vic) leaned into the play’s expressionistic dimension: the set designer Anna Fleischle suggested the house by busily flying in window frames, doorways, and even some furniture from above when needed; the director, Miranda Cromwell, interpolated songs that heightened the play’s emotional effect. Sharon D. Clarke, a stunning, stoic Linda, ended the closing scene at Willy’s grave with a haunting gospel tune.

In the current production, Mantello pulls the play even more forcefully—and more fruitfully—toward abstraction. In place of the standard house, he and the set designer Chloe Lamford have constructed a vast, warehouse-like nowhere. Setting—kitchen, bedroom, restaurant, office, hotel room, yard, cemetery—is fluidly evoked by a table or chair here, a couple of steel benches there, a partially dirt-strewn floor, a lonely upstage refrigerator. Pillars that have shed much of their tiling are arrayed across the wide space, lending some vertical lift as well as suggesting aspiration and its disintegration. Along the edges, barely discernible objects—a tricycle, a watering can—sometimes catch a shaft of light, memorabilia of the family’s past that drift in and out of Willy’s mind.

An oversized garage door fills the upstage-center wall, and the play opens with headlights beaming right into our eyes as—for the first time in any Broadway production—Willy drives his car onstage. It stays parked there for almost the entire two and three-quarter hours of the show, source and symbol of both Willy’s livelihood and his demise. Characters sometimes enter from or exit into it; Linda rests a coffee pot on its hood; teenage Biff strides atop its roof vowing to run for a touchdown in his upcoming game. In the penultimate scene, the garage door slides open and Willy backs out—of the space, of life.

The car is one of many anachronistic elements that make time as fluid as space in this production. Though the text tells us that Willy has replaced his old Chevy with a Studebaker, what we see is a sleek Chevrolet—the automobile whose famous slogan summons us, like the play itself, to “see the USA.” While that tagline emerged in the late 1940s, contemporaneous with Salesman, the model on stage is a 1964 Chevelle, a famed “muscle car” known for those made-in-America ideals of high performance and quick acceleration.

Other details also suggest the sweep of the last eighty years, further widening the play’s metaphoric scope. A half-gallon carton of Organic Valley milk sits on the table. In Rudy Mance’s costuming, Willy wears a timeless department-store brown suit and Linda, at the beginning of Act Two, contemporary black slacks and a teal blouse, a color trendy at midcentury, in the 1990s, and again now. In the excruciating scene in which Willy grovels before his young boss, Howard (John Drea), begging not to be fired, Drea wears a tech-bro vest over his shirt and tie and sips from a paper coffee cup he might have picked up around the corner during intermission. The point isn’t to hammer what we already know about today’s rapacious robber barons but to subsume us in the long arc of profit-driven cruelty.

This permeability of time reflects Willy’s mental state. He lives at once in an idealized past and an untenable present. Subtle shifts in Jack Knowles’s atmospheric lighting—between amber warmth and steely starkness—demarcate these realms. But Willy makes no distinction as he crosses his personal time zones. Breaking from the tradition that began with Elia Kazan’s storied premiere production, in which actors playing Biff, Happy, and their neighboring classmate Bernard portrayed the characters both as adult men and as teenagers, Mantello cast additional actors to play the boys in their youth. We see them, then, as Willy remembers them. (Miller’s pre-production draft, which Mantello consulted, calls for separate actors for the younger and older sons.) Often the two Biffs and Haps occupy the stage at the same time, conveying a woeful sense of the grown men’s squandered potential and the unshakeable specter of the past in the present. We carry this perception into the devastating final face-off between father and son—in which Biff breaks down as he tries in vain to persuade Willy to “take that phony dream and burn it.”

A significant strain of criticism of Miller, in the decades since Salesman’s premiere, has involved his female characters. A generation of feminist scholars pulled apart his tendency to present women as either helpmates or temptresses, never protagonists. In a much-cited essay from 1989, Kay Stanton argued that “the American Dream as presented in Death of a Salesman is male-oriented, but it requires unacknowledged dependence upon women as well as women’s subjugation and exploitation.” In a mid-1990s cover-story takedown of Miller in London’s The Sunday Times, Rhoda Koenig famously called Linda “a dumb and useful doormat.”

That sharp criticism has dulled with the years, however, especially as actors have brought layers of strength and complexity to Miller’s roles. The last decade has also seen a spate of dramaturgical rejoinders, additive rather than censorious works that take off from Salesman to offer Linda’s character a different path: Eleanor Burgess’s prequel to Miller’s drama, Wife of a Salesman; Barbara Cassidy’s sequel, Mrs. Loman; and Katie Forgette’s backstage comedy, Mrs. Loman is Leaving. (Another half-dozen such works pick up on The Crucible, most prominently Kimberly Belflower’s John Proctor is the Villain, a nominee for the best-play Tony last year.)

Thanks to Laurie Metcalf’s performance, Mantello’s production tacitly joins this trend. Her Linda is tenacious, tender, complex: the family mainstay, packed with tamped-down frustrations and practiced good cheer. We recognize that it takes labor not only to keep the household accounts, but also to shore up her flailing husband. She accepts her job—and excels at it—without bitterness or self-pity.

Meanwhile, at a time when the nation speaks officially in the register of bluster, braggadocio, and hostile barbs, the Loman men seem all too familiar. Willy lies, browbeats, contradicts himself, badgers others into repeating his fantasy version of the truth. Lane strikes a properly wobbly balance between depicting a despairing man who has lost his grip on reality and a megalomaniacal one trying to force others to accept his sham version of it; he’s both sympathetic and repellent. The play brims with violent rhetoric: Willy boasts, falsely, that on his sales trips he “knocked ’em cold in Providence, slaughtered them in Boston.” The value system he imparts to his sons, too, measures human worth in dollars and defines success—and masculinity—as the vanquishing of others: “You guys together could absolutely lick the civilized world,” he tells them. Happy, pumping himself up in his father’s mode (with jaunty insouciance in Ben Ahlers’s portrayal), describes his pursuit of women as “like bowling or something. I just keep knockin’ them over and it doesn’t mean anything.”

In contrast, Biff, long disillusioned by his father’s infidelity, struggles to purge the poison Willy has pumped into him. Christopher Abbott plays the adrift thirty-four-year-old as coiled up with frustration, struggling to contain an impulse to strike out. It’s both shocking and strangely satisfying when he almost does so: as Willy eggs Biff on, advising him on how to seek a business loan, he barks at Linda to “stop interrupting.” Biff springs up, crying, “Stop yelling at her!” and cocks his fist. Where Willy’s efforts to bat Linda away were likely once read simply as underscoring his delusional bullishness, today they come out slathered with sexism.

The production’s most surprising innovation is to not only foreground Willy’s misogyny but spotlight its part in what bell hooks long ago called “white-supremacist capitalist patriarchy.” In an unconventional casting choice, black actors play Willy’s generous neighbor, Charley (K. Todd Freeman), and Charley’s hardworking son, Bernard (Michael Benjamin Washington as an adult; Karl Green as a teenager). Willy’s envy of them, then, reeks of white grievance. When Willy turns down a job offer from Charley, his refusal—“I just can’t work for you”—reads as repugnant racial pride.

Linda, in Metcalf’s masterly portrayal, is the only one who understands not just that Willy has misplaced his faith in a noxious system—as Biff also grasps—but also what produces its toxicity. She describes him to Biff as “only a little boat looking for a harbor”—an inchoate recognition of the storm that bandies him about. In the closing funeral scene, which Miller titled “Requiem,” she grieves Willy’s death, to be sure. But Metcalf offers a glimmer of possibility in those last words, along with an innovative gesture: she buries a paper—presumably the paid-off mortgage deed—with her husband. I couldn’t help feeling that for all her sadness, Linda realizes that she, herself, is now free.

entries.content:
In “The Art of the Interview,” season four of the podcast The Critic and Her Publics, Merve Emre speaks with top writers and journalists to discuss the subtle skill of conducting an interview. The Review is collaborating with Lit Hub to publish transcripts and recordings of each episode.

Sarah Stillman is a staff writer at The New Yorker and one of the most decorated investigative reporters of her generation. She has won several National Magazine Awards, the Pulitzer Prize, and a MacArthur “Genius” Grant. Her work draws attention to the men and women forced to do the bidding of the American security state—the so-called “third-country nationals” who were tricked into working on military bases in Iraq, the addicts coerced into serving as police informants, and the victims of civil-asset forfeiture.

Our conversation, the third episode of “The Art of the Interview,” touched on every stage of Stillman’s career, from her days as a student journalist to her current directorship of Yale’s Investigative Reporting Lab, where she helps students cultivate the relentlessness and compassion that make her a uniquely effective reporter.

Merve Emre: Most of the people in this room are college students who might look to you as an example of how a journalist can make a career. Could you tell us about how you got to where you are today?

Sarah Stillman: I got my reporting start when I was at the Yale gym my senior year, trying to figure out what I was going to do my senior thesis about. They were playing Fox News on the TV, and there was a story in Florida about this young girl, Jessica Lunsford, who went missing. Hundreds of people had come to try to find her. This was in the Nancy Grace era when there was nonstop coverage of missing and murdered white women. The news ticker on the screen said that the body found in the lake was not Jessica, and it was presented as good news.

Of course, that raised some big questions for me. Who was this other body? At the time, I was taking an investigative reporting class where I was learning about public records, so I went back to my dorm, called the sheriff’s office, and asked for the name of the body in the lake. They told me her name was Donna Joan Cook, and I did a public-record search and found that she had been repeatedly convicted of sex work–related charges starting when she was young.

My senior project became going to Florida and figuring out this young woman’s story. Ultimately, I learned that because she had mental health issues that were preventing her from paying off her fines, she had agreed to work as a confidential informant for the police. She started getting death threats from someone who she had essentially ratted out, and wound up dead soon after. My first journalistic inquiry was trying to tell not only this young woman’s story, but also how we got to a world where we have the Jessicas and the not-Jessicas. That became central to my whole reporting career—we’re trained to look at the “main story” that everyone is paying attention to in the headlines, but embedded within that are stories that have been pushed to the side.

Many people, upon seeing that news ticker, would have just kept working out. They would not have thought to call the sheriff’s office and get the name and look through the public records. Do you remember what made you want to do that?

I am a physical reporter. I pay a lot of attention to my own body; where am I curious, where am I surprised? So many of my story ideas have come out of seeing something in the news that doesn’t feel right and wanting to do some further digging. I was taking this reporting course with the amazing Bruce Shapiro, who had us each draw a piece of paper out of a hat, and we had to tell a story strictly based upon the address on the paper. Mine wound up being about a nursing home that had burned down in New Haven. There had been litigation around it, and I learned about this universe of things that were accessible. Often, we think of investigative work as someone uncovering a deep, dark secret that no one had access to, but most of the time, the compelling investigative stories are already out there in the public sphere, in dots that haven’t been looked at as a constellation. For me, that means almost always, if you’re curious, something deeper is there. Trusting my intuition has proved both helpful and really gratifying.

After you finished this piece for your college project, what happened?

I was a freshman in college when the Iraq War began. It was a big part of my formation as a journalist. I knew I wanted to do something tied to the reality that the US was in two wars by the time that I graduated, but I didn’t feel qualified to dive into investigative reporting in Iraq. I didn’t speak Arabic, I didn’t have a deep understanding of Iraqi history, and I didn’t want to parachute into a situation I was not sufficiently equipped for. So I thought about Bruce’s advice to think about your comparative advantage in any given terrain. I come from a family of labor organizers, and they’ve always taught me to think about what the experiences of working people are in any storytelling ecosystem.

Advertisement

When it came to the Iraq War, again, I’d seen some headlines about a group of Nepali workers who thought they had been recruited to work in fancy hotels in Jordan and Dubai, but were in fact en route to do logistics work on a US military base. I found it wasn’t just a few people; the US had brought some 60,000 people in from Sierra Leone, Uganda, Sri Lanka, all around the world to do these jobs, and often, those people were lied to. That is another example of a piece that was at the margins of a conventional story.

That became the premise of the first piece you ever wrote for The New Yorker, “The Invisible Army.” You tell the story of two beauticians from Fiji who have been recruited into doing service work for the US army in Iraq when they thought they would be working at a salon in Dubai. How do you decide who the main characters are going to be in a piece?

That was a major journey, because I had no idea what I was doing. I arrived at the largest US military base in Baghdad, and instantaneously, when you arrive, you see a Cinnabon and Pizza Hut and a beauty salon staffed entirely by people who had been recruited there.

How did you end up on the US military base?

I was an embed with a military police unit in Iraq. At the time the military offered journalists a chance to work alongside US military forces. In my case, I had to do that to get on to the base. I didn’t think it’d be the best idea to say to the government, “I would like to investigate your human trafficking practices. Can I come hang out with you?” So I simultaneously did stories for the official embedment and reported on this trafficking issue. At the beginning, I wasn’t savvy about approaching people in the right spaces. I went into the beauty salon, thinking, I’ll just get a manicure and quietly ask some questions. They said they loved their jobs, that they were so lucky to be here. I quickly realized I could not ask things in the vicinity of their employers.

There was a bus circulating around the base, driven by a Sri Lankan guy. I started chatting with him. Like the women in the salon, he kept saying “Everything is great! We’re very happy here.” I saw him again and again, and finally, one night, I was on the bus when no one else was on it, and he broke down in tears. “This is a horrific situation, we were lied to about why we’re here. There are loan sharks coming after my family and the families around us, chasing down the money we paid to get the jobs, our passports were taken,” a whole litany of horrors. Once I learned the right way to do it, I spoke to more than a hundred people, almost all of whom had a horrific story of their recruitment and what they’d faced on the base.

The reason I chose to go with the Fijian women is that they had lived the arc of the experience. They had been approached at beauty salons in their home countries with someone promising them $3,800 a month and they agreed. Instead, they went to a transit country and then found out they were going to Iraq. One of them was sexually assaulted by her employer. I was able to follow the full trajectory to when they got home and were safely situated. Oftentimes, it’s complex reporting terrain when people have reasons to feel afraid of telling their stories, and a lot of the process is figuring out who’s in a safe position to talk, and who wants to talk. And these women really wanted their stories to be known.

How do you get people to trust you?

A lot of it is being alongside them in their day-to-day experiences. I wound up being in some critical moments with them, including the night that one of them was assaulted. I went to her containerized housing unit, basically a shipping container, where they all lived. When they opened the door, one of them was crying and explained what had happened. All around the base, I had seen these posters for the military sexual assault hotline, but these women didn’t have access to that type of phone, because you had to be a service member or have access to US media sources to get it, so they asked me if I’d be willing to call. In journalism, you’re taught not to get involved, but my ethos has always been showing up, first and foremost, as a human. So I called the emergency hotline, and no one answered. I called repeatedly, and finally, when I got through, they told me to call the company. So I called the company, and they said, “We don’t handle touchy-feely issues. Call the military.” I was with these women in some intense processes, and that was bonding glue. But with a lot of stories, I ask people if I can follow along for the softer moments in the day. It’s meaningful trust, building time.

That’s interesting, because for many of the people we’ve spoken with, the interview requires a setup that is different from the movement of day-to-day life.

I would feel so panicked if I had one chance to do an interview. What I’m seeking in an interview is earning the right to return—establishing care, rapport, trust, and mutual interest so that we can have many conversations thereafter.

There are two ways that you’re very present in that piece. One is the moment when you call the sexual assault hotline, and the other is when, based on your investigation, an inquiry is opened into the status of these women back in Washington, D.C. I’m curious about what it’s like when your presence as a reporter changes the direction the story takes. How do you think of balancing the journalist in you with the labor activist or feminist activist?

It was panic inducing, because I had been working on this story for a year, and I got a call from a Washington Post reporter who had found a PowerPoint slide the military was using internally, which said that they had found out about this human trafficking incident a journalist was alleging. They called me to investigate the story. I had been roundly rejected after I had gone to Iraq, gone to Afghanistan, found hundreds of people who could testify to being starved or abused on US bases. I thought that would be sufficient, but I was rejected by the publications I’d sent it out to, which said that people had war fatigue. They also had a hard time taking a risk on a young journalist. I met this guy who said, “You should just write the Platonic ideal of the piece that you want to write.” So I sat down and crafted that version of the story.

When the US government got involved and changed the course of the investigation, I benefited tremendously because I was a young journalist who did not know the art of the interview. I had been nervous to ask the core questions you have to ask to craft a granular narrative. I felt like it was too personal and I didn’t want to violate someone’s privacy or retraumatize them. But one of the Fijian women, Vinnie, was brought to the US and met with lawyers at the State Department who were looking into whether they could sue on her behalf. They let me come to the meeting where the lawyers interviewed her, and the art of the interview for a litigator is an incredible thing to watch. They do the thing that Seymour Hersh talks about, “the chron,” which is just mapping out the sequence of events. They start at the very beginning, “Who came to you in the salon?” “What did he look like?” “What was he wearing?” They went through a thousand questions I would have never asked. But Vinnie started talking in a different way, and it taught me the dialectical nature of the interview.

You start being curious, respectful but mindful that there may be areas the person doesn’t want to cover. I’ve learned a practice of setting the table, saying, “I would love to hear everything that you’re willing to share. If we hit upon realms where you don’t want to talk about it, that’s okay too”—putting the agency very explicitly back in the other person’s hands but trusting them to go there. At this point in my job, I’ve learned how deeply people want to be heard, and how when you start asking the granular questions, people rise to the occasion. That has been a beautiful thing for me to learn from and really transformed how I think about interviews.

What did you learn from that first foray into interviewing, reporting, writing the story, and having it edited and released?

I learned how to be more organized, because if you take on a project that spans months or years, you have to file interviews and PDFs, photographs, the full terrain. Also, because I’m a massive over-reporter and over-interviewer, I learned to boil it down to my rule of five: What are the five things that have to come through in the story, and who are the people within it that can carry me from the beginning to the end?

How do you deal with difficult and resistant subjects?

I’m not good at getting the problematic figures in a piece to talk. When I was reporting in Iraq, they treated me like I was writing for the student newspaper. When I was younger, I would constantly be dismissed. Then I realized that’s a real asset. They are blowing you off and allowing you to wander about, and they can’t even fathom that someone who looked as I did at the time could be doing substantive investigative work. Navigating the frustrations of that was fruitful in certain ways.

What you’ve articulated is essentially the Joan Didion school of reporting, which is, the more you make yourself seem as if you’re small and unserious, or feminized, the more people will reveal in front of you without thinking twice about what they’re revealing.

I wish I could say I did it the Joan Didion way. I worked so hard to be taken seriously, but it still didn’t happen, so I just went with it. Some of the best quotes I’ve gotten have been from people explaining why they can’t talk to me. If someone just went through a traumatic experience and said they didn’t want to talk and explained why, I would treat that as off the record. But in the case of people who have perpetrated serious harms against others and explain why they can’t talk to me, that’s not off the record. I did a piece on civil-asset forfeiture where this police department in Texas was pulling over almost every driver of color who passed through, checking if they had cash in the car and threatening to send those people’s kids into foster care if they didn’t let them seize the cash and sign it away. In that case, the officer who was leading the ring gave me a thirty-minute explanation of why he couldn’t talk to me that included how he’d gotten messages from God about how he had to seize their money. I wound up using that in the piece.

I almost never go into an interview thinking about it in the reductive way I just presented, “the other side.” I find that most of the time, people are complex actors who are not inherently malicious. I’m really interested in what motivated someone who was part of a system engaged in, for instance, profiteering. I’ve had some fruitful and surprising interviews, and a huge key is to not make assumptions. I hate reporting that feels like someone had a preexisting equation. I am genuinely interested in what animates all the actors in a piece and I try to read the drafts while projecting my imagination into the minds of the different figures involved, including the folks accused of something serious. At The New Yorker, we have a no surprises policy; we call people in the fact-checking process. I love that because often you’ll learn rich things when calling to confront someone about something serious that they’re accused of. You learn more layers to the story, and that is valuable, not just lip service.

You’ve done a lot of reporting recently on family separation and deportation. Do you approach interview subjects who are young and vulnerable in a different way?

That’s a really complicated one. I’ve been thinking a lot about what informed consent really means, not just when someone’s a child, but in recent circumstances in which the situation one is in has its own coercive power. I worked on a piece about the Trump administration’s secretive third-country deportations, and I got a call on a Saturday morning from a military detention camp in Ghana. There were eleven people on the phone call, and all of them were in absolute terror. Sweat was streaming down their faces; they looked the most afraid of anyone I’ve ever interviewed.

They were people who had, in many cases, lived in the US for a long time. Some of them were more recent asylum seekers, including several women who had fled female genital mutilation in Togo. They’d gotten protection from being sent back to Togo in a US immigration court, and this administration chose to send them to Ghana, which was going to send them back to their home country. The moment I spoke to them, they were trying to get a journalist to write about their predicament, because they feared they were about to be sent back.

That situation was almost more complicated than interviewing children. If I had spoken to them prior to their deportation, they would never have wanted to speak about their immigration circumstances. But I caught them in this moment when they had a profound, urgent, truly life-threatening need, and that made them willing to speak. It made me think about the complex politics of what it means for someone to consent.

With kids, it’s important to brainstorm how we build proper safeguards for the reporting. Kids can bring forth so many creative ideas that can resonate with a reader about the consequences of this administration’s policies. I did a project some years ago about people who had come to the US seeking asylum, who got deported, and then were killed or harmed after their deportations. I wrote about a woman in Texas, Laura, and her family who had lived here for many years. She had an abusive ex-partner who had been deported to Mexico. She got pulled over for a minor traffic violation and while she had two children who were US citizens, she was sent back across the border the same day. When they deported her, she told the border officers verbatim, “When I’m killed next week, my blood will be on your hands.” And that’s exactly what happened.

I went down there and spent time with Laura’s mother and with her kids. One of the ways I wrote about that in the piece, thinking about how to both honor their experience and not violate their privacy, was sharing some writings that the kids had done for their mom. They had an annual tradition where they each wrote a poem, put them on balloons, and released them. One of the kids had also written a separate poem that he was willing to share. I thought that would be one way to kind of incorporate his voice in a way that he felt proud of.

You’re very good at incorporating voices that other reporters might not necessarily think about bringing in. I am so impressed by your piece on the felony murder doctrine, “Sentenced to Life for an Accident Miles Away,” because on the one hand, you are speaking to a person convicted of felony murder, and on the other, you’re speaking to the stepson of his alleged victim, who doesn’t believe in the felony murder doctrine and finds it to be unjust. One of the most impressive things about that piece is your movement between those two subjects. There’s a kinship you unearth between them, even though they ought to be on opposite sides of the issue. I’m curious to hear how that piece came about and how your conversations with them led to the structure.

For years I’d wanted to write about the felony murder doctrine. It’s a law that states that people involved in a felony where someone dies, even if they weren’t present, can be convicted of first-degree murder with mandatory life in prison without parole. I knew of many interesting cases, and I’d always been looking for the right one. Then a friend told me about Ian Marcus, with whom I start the piece. In that case, two young men in Florida went out to a casino and lost a bunch of money, so they were taking loose change and minor items from unlocked vehicles. A neighbor saw them and called the police, who came and arrested one of the guys, Sadik Baxter. While they put him in handcuffs, his friend was in his vehicle and fled, winding up in a high-speed chase with the police during which he hit and killed two bicyclists, one of whom was Ian’s father.

Sadik was prosecuted for two first-degree murders, even though he was not at the scene, because of the felony murder doctrine. Ian and his family were upset about this, because not only had they lost their father, but Sadik was going to lose his ability to be with his kid. It was this profound illustration of how the doctrine worked and why it feels bizarre. The judge himself said, “My hands are tied, but I don’t think this makes sense.” I called Ian, he said he wasn’t ready to talk, maybe someday, but not right now. I followed up a year later, and he was ready to talk, as were his sisters. I also found my way to Sadik’s family and to Sadik in prison. It was confusing, because at first he was so excited to talk to me: “Oh my God, I’ve been searching for years for a journalist. I wrote to Kim Kardashian, I wrote to Barack Obama, and no one has gotten back to me. I was hoping to find someone.” But then, as we started the interviews, he was monosyllabic. It was the inverse of every other interview; he was down to talk about the case, but not about his personal life.

Why do you think that was?

I truly was exasperated; I almost gave up. To make a New Yorker story work, you want to feel like all parties want to be talking to you, it won’t work if they’re not. In a last-ditch effort, I flew down to Florida to visit him in prison in Okaloosa. It is not an easy place to get to; he had not had a visitor in five years. I got a rental car, I drove down, and everything opened up from there. He’s one of the most creative, interesting, amazing conversationalists I’ve ever known. He explained that he was aware there’s a private security company that listens to all phone calls when you’re incarcerated. For-profit phone companies have commandeered the phone lines, so it’s both very expensive and hyper-surveilled. He hated the idea that after being screwed over by so many systems, they would now have access to all his intimate life.

I also was turned away three times because of the pants that I was wearing. The first guard said they were scandalous. I came back in black pants, and they said those pants were see-through in the hot Florida sun. I changed into a third pair, which they said were not see-through but could become see-through if I started to sweat. I was losing my mind. But luckily, with his help negotiating and my own pleading, I got in to see him. I think in that whole process, he recognized that I was who I said I was.

What pants did you end up wearing?

The white pants, and they were right about them being see-through when I sweat. I also thought I’d pulled a trick on them, because they took away my paper and pen, so I asked them for a copy of the prison’s rules about clothing, turned it over, and used it as my notepad. But they took that away too. It was a reminder that they don’t want interviewing happening in those spaces, and don’t want to give incarcerated people the right to share their stories openly.

It has been interesting to hear from our guests about the circumstances in which people do not want interviews to take place. How has your approach to interviewing changed between the Obama administration, the first Trump administration, and the second Trump administration?

I have learned helpful lessons from my own reporting failures during the first Trump administration. I fell into a state of severe existential despair, wondering if I was just becoming a vehicle for them to distribute more fear and terror. Those questions remain for me, but in watching what unfolded with the family separation crisis, I learned that this administration is always testing the boundaries of what they can get away with, and sometimes, they hit those boundaries when communities take to the streets.

For family separation work, I had just finished a story about a woman in Texas, which I had begun at the tail end of the Obama years, about people being deported to their deaths. Soon thereafter, Trump took office. I started looking into the decimation of asylum policy. I’d found some early accounts of people who’d been separated and was trying to figure out if it was something we could write about. My editor said we should check with the administration to see if it was a formal policy. I went to the administration, and they said they were not doing it. I actually believed them, because they were loudly owning their immigration enforcement policies. The following spring, they unveiled the zero-tolerance prosecutions and started the widespread practice of family separations. Thanks to incredible reporting by folks like Caitlin Dickerson, we learned that they had been doing early testing of that policy to see if they could get away with it. When they did it on a large scale, we saw a lot of incredible reporting, and tons of mass protests with people taking to the streets. We’re seeing that again with what’s unfolded in the immigration enforcement actions in LA, Chicago, and Minneapolis, but it has taken the killing of two white US citizens, one of them being a male gun owner, to begin to hit up against the boundaries.

We cannot underestimate the power of what it takes for both incredible organizers and the people who are directly affected to have the courage to tell stories with more tools than ever, which I think is an incredibly influential and important part of the media ecosystem right now, but it also takes deep investigative reporting. There are a lot of things told to the public, but there’s always the secret layer. With third-country deportations, they told a lot publicly, tweeting about “deporting the worst of the worst,” sending them to Eswatini or Ghana, but beneath that, there was the secrecy unveiled by reporting, like the financial deals made with these countries. We need both the people who are willing to come forth and share their stories, and we need the journalism that’s going to unearth that. I’ve never felt as deeply or seen as much evidence for why we need reporting.

entries.title: Close Calls
entries.summary: In the Supreme Court’s recently concluded term, it showed that it is willing to constrain Trump but less willing to accept limits on its own authority.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Can we rely on the courts, and most importantly the Supreme Court, to resist major assaults on the rule of law by the Trump administration? That question was front and center during the Court’s recently concluded 2025–2026 term. With its six Republican appointees—three nominated by Trump—some feared that, much like the Republican-controlled Congress, the Court would reflexively back the president. Initial indications from the Court’s “emergency docket,” where it considers requests to temporarily stay lower court orders, seemed to bear out those worries. The Court has granted seventeen such requests, often without giving any reasons and usually by a 6–3 margin.

By the end of the term, however, the story was more nuanced. The Court blocked four of Trump’s major initiatives: ending birthright citizenship, imposing worldwide tariffs, firing Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, and dispatching National Guard troops to Chicago, Portland, and other cities. In other significant cases as well, the Court rejected positions advanced by Trump. In a decision that he called “a tremendous loss,” it held that federal law permits the counting of mail-in ballots posted by election day but received thereafter. And it refuted the Trump administration’s assertion of constitutionally unchecked power to demand that Google turn over the cell phone location histories of unlimited numbers of Americans. The justices may not be, as Trump called them after he lost the tariffs case, “fools and lapdogs for the RINOs and the radical left Democrats,” but this is not Donald Trump’s Court.

Each of Trump’s appointees voted against him on important issues. In the tariffs case, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch, both Trump appointees, as well as Chief Justice John Roberts joined the three Democratic appointees—Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor, and Ketanji Brown Jackson—to rule against the president. In the birthright citizenship case, Barrett, Roberts, and Brett Kavanaugh, another Trump appointee, joined the three liberal justices to reject Trump’s attempt to redefine who is an American. Roberts, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch joined the liberals to find that the federal government’s demand for cell phone location data is a search limited by the Fourth Amendment. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the three liberal justices to block Trump’s firing of Cook. And in the National Guard case, Kavanaugh, Barrett, and Roberts joined the liberals. These are not the decisions of a Court doing the president’s bidding or voting exclusively along party lines. By contrast, had these issues been put to a vote in Congress, would a single Republican have broken ranks?

The rulings cannot be dismissed as mere token losses for Trump. Each one established important guardrails on the executive branch. The tariffs decision rejected the president’s assertion of emergency powers, a step courts rarely take. Justice Samuel Alito called the birthright citizenship case “one of the most important decisions in the history of the Court.” The decision blocking the firing of Cook protected the independence of the Federal Reserve, the nation’s most powerful financial institution. And the National Guard decision kept troops off our streets, halting Trump’s invocation of a classic authoritarian move.

Nor can the decisions be discounted on the ground that no reasonable judge could rule in Trump’s favor. They all raised serious and unresolved questions. In Trump v. Barbara, the Court ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment, which extends citizenship to all persons born in the United States and “subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” was intended to adopt the then-existing common law rule of birthright citizenship. That rule, borrowed from English common law, provided that virtually all persons born in the country were “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” and therefore citizens, with only four narrow exceptions: children of ambassadors, people born in territory occupied by a foreign power, individuals born on foreign ships, and Native Americans born on tribal lands. (Congress subsequently extended citizenship to Native Americans by statute.)

In 1898 the Court affirmed this common law understanding in United States v. Wong Kim Ark. But that case involved the child of Chinese nationals who were permanently and legally domiciled in the United States, so it did not technically involve the classes of persons to whom Trump sought to deny citizenship: children of foreign nationals here illegally and children of transient visitors.

While six justices agreed that Trump’s executive order was illegal, only five (Roberts, Barrett, and the three liberals) deemed it unconstitutional. Kavanaugh concurred only because Congress had incorporated the common law understanding into statute in 1940 and 1952, and he concluded that Trump’s order violated that statute. But on the constitutional question, Barbara turned out to be a close case; four justices concluded that the Constitution permitted Trump’s interpretation. Alito and Kavanaugh reasoned that neither the framers of the Fourteenth Amendment nor the Court in Wong Kim Ark had considered the issue of illegally or temporarily present foreign nationals. When the Fourteenth Amendment was adopted, there were no restrictions on immigration, so there were no “illegal aliens,” and the logistics of travel meant that transient visitors were rare. Thomas and Gorsuch viewed the Fourteenth Amendment as addressed principally to the citizenship of the newly freed slaves, who were both born and “domiciled” here; they therefore found that it did not encompass temporary or illegal visitors. The majority had the stronger argument from precedent, principle, and what you might call legal culture: it has long been the settled understanding that virtually everyone born here is a citizen, and that rule is both simple to administer and puts everyone on an equal footing from birth. But the dissents raise serious objections that cannot be dismissed out of hand, as the nearly two hundred pages of opinions attest.1

Advertisement

The tariffs case also presented a close question. The majority ruled that the president’s power to “regulate” imports under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) does not include the power to impose tariffs, as the Constitution generally assigns the power to tax to Congress, a tariff is a type of tax, and the IEEPA does not explicitly delegate the authority to tariff to the president. But Kavanaugh wrote a thoughtful dissent for three justices that echoed an earlier decision by Judge Richard Taranto, a widely respected moderate member of the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. The Supreme Court had previously interpreted the IEEPA broadly, and President Richard Nixon had imposed tariffs under a predecessor statute. Reasonable people could differ on the legal question, yet the Court sided against the president.

In Trump v. Cook, the majority ruled that the president does not have unilateral authority to remove governors from the Federal Reserve Board, even though in another case the same day, it recognized such an authority over virtually all other federal agencies. The Court identified no principled rationale for the distinction. It simply noted that the Federal Reserve is a successor of sorts to the First and Second Banks of the United States, which were independent of the executive. But those predecessors exercised substantially less authority than the Fed does today, so the agency’s historical provenance does not offer a rational justification for treating it differently from other agencies today. The Court also rejected Trump’s argument that his determination that Cook was properly dismissed “for cause” was not judicially reviewable and that Cook had been provided adequate notice and opportunity to respond. But there was very little precedent on these questions, and the vote was 5–4, as close as it gets, so again the case cannot be considered an inevitable defeat for the president.

In Chatrie v. United States, the Court declared that the federal government’s use of a “geofence warrant” to obtain personal cell phone location data from Google on anyone in the vicinity of a bank when it was robbed amounted to a search governed by the Fourth Amendment. The Trump administration argued that the Fourth Amendment did not apply at all, meaning that the government could demand location history without any warrant or probable cause. It urged the Court to extend analog-era precedents holding that bank records and pen registers, which record the phone numbers you call, are not protected by the Fourth Amendment because when you open a bank account or use a phone, you voluntarily give that information to the bank or phone company, forfeiting any privacy. Applying that rule to digital information, however, would have disastrous implications, as nowadays we share virtually everything we do with a third party—our emails, photos, texts, documents, Google searches, online reading habits, and physical location. The Court ruled that location data is sufficiently personal and revealing, and not truly voluntarily shared, to warrant Fourth Amendment protection. But this was a novel question, and three justices dissented.

In yet another significant loss for the administration, the Court upheld the counting of mail-in ballots postmarked by election day but received thereafter. The Trump administration argued that only votes received by election day could be counted, invoking (as is the president’s wont) the largely chimerical prospect of voter fraud. Many observers of the oral argument expected the Court to rule with the president, and the case raised difficult questions about what constitutes an “election.” The Court ultimately sided against the president. In short, these were all close cases, and if the Court were merely seeking to do Trump’s bidding, it could have ruled his way in all of them.

Many skeptics of the Court’s independence cite the administration’s lopsided winning percentage on the emergency docket. The Court has granted temporary stays of lower court orders in major disputes involving his efforts to halt USAID funding, fire agency heads, decimate agency staffs, and subject people in Los Angeles who look Latino or speak Spanish to forcible stops by ICE agents. But here, too, the story is complicated. The Court has denied the administration’s requests for stays, not only in the National Guard and Lisa Cook cases but also with respect to Trump’s effort to deport Venezuelans without hearings under the Alien Enemies Act and his foot-dragging in bringing back Kilmar Armando Ábrego García, an erroneously deported Salvadoran.

Advertisement

In addition, as the Harvard Law School professor Jack Goldsmith has pointed out, Trump’s relatively high win ratio on the emergency docket is partly attributable to the fact that Solicitor General John Sauer has been strategic about which lower court rulings he asks the Supreme Court to stay.2 Lower federal courts have issued at least 150 injunctions against the Trump administration, including ordering the Kennedy Center to remove his name from the building’s official title, blocking efforts to limit mail-in ballots and subpoena voter records, overturning the defunding of National Public Radio and the Public Broadcasting Service, barring the administration from denying funds to Harvard, and nullifying its efforts to punish law firms Trump doesn’t like. On one legal issue alone, whether the administration can detain immigrants without a bond hearing while their removal cases are pending, more than four hundred judges have said no and ordered bond hearings or release for more than 10,000 foreign nationals. The solicitor general has not sought emergency Supreme Court review in any of these cases. Had he done so, the administration’s win–loss ratio would look very different.

But while the Court has demonstrated its willingness to enforce limits against Trump, it recognizes few limits on its own power. In particular, it too often runs roughshod over prior decisions to achieve conservative results simply because it disagrees with those prior decisions. Stare decisis, the obligation to follow precedent, is critical to judicial legitimacy, but this Court treats it as optional. Sometimes it overrules prior decisions outright; more often it just declines to follow inconvenient precedent. Since the addition of Trump’s three appointees, the Court has already eliminated women’s right to abortion, ended affirmative action, compelled state and local governments to support discrimination by religious entities, and imposed newfound restrictions on the regulation of guns. This term, the Court’s most consequential conservative results involved the president’s power to fire agency heads, campaign finance law, the rights of trans girls and women to participate in sports, immigration enforcement, and voting rights. Each decision reached a conservative outcome by a 6–3 margin, often in the face of precedents strongly supporting the opposite result. So while the conservatives may not be doing Trump’s bidding, they are pursuing their own ideological aims, often heedless of precedent.

In Trump v. Slaughter, for example, the Court overturned Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, a unanimous 1935 decision that upheld statutory limits on the president’s power to remove the heads of independent agencies, so called because Congress concluded that their responsibilities warranted some degree of protection from absolute presidential control. Humphrey’s Executor and Slaughter involved the statute governing the Federal Trade Commission, which provided that the president could remove a commissioner only “for cause,” namely for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance, but not simply because of a policy disagreement. Congress has imposed similar constraints on other agencies that it believes should exercise independent judgment, such as the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Federal Reserve Board.

The Constitution specifies that agency heads must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, giving Congress an important part in the appointment process. But it says nothing about removal of officers. In other circumstances, this Court has insisted that it has no authority to limit the political branches when the Constitution is silent—as in the case of abortion. The decision to leave the removal power unspecified might be read as allowing the matter to be worked out between the president and Congress. In Humphrey’s Executor, the Court ruled that if an agency exercises quasi-judicial or quasi-legislative functions, in this case adjudicating law violations and promulgating regulations, Congress could impose a “for cause” limit on the president’s ability to fire the heads of such agencies. Congress has relied on that precedent for nearly a century.

In Slaughter, the Court reversed course and held that all heads of executive agencies must serve at the whim of the president, with the sole exception, at least thus far, of governors of the Federal Reserve. Despite its ostensible commitment to textualism, the only constitutional words it cited were a question-begging provision that vests “the executive power” in the president and another that obligates him to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” Neither clause says anything about firing officials at will. But the majority maintained that if the president is to execute the laws, he has to have untrammeled ability to fire officers for any reason.

This conclusion certainly is not required by the meager text to which the Court pointed. The president executes the laws every day in accordance with the conditions and limits that Congress enacts; the fact that he must abide by those constraints doesn’t mean that he is not exercising executive power or faithfully executing the laws. Nor does it mean that Congress is impermissibly executing the laws itself.

Past precedents have recognized that there are often good reasons for Congress to want its laws to be administered by someone who is not entirely subject to the president’s whim. In Morrison v. Olson (1988), for example, the Court, in a 7–1 decision written by Chief Justice William Rehnquist—no liberal—upheld a “for cause” restriction on the firing of the independent counsel. The Court found that Congress had reasonably decided that when serious allegations of crime by the president or cabinet officials needed to be investigated, it should be done with some degree of insulation from the president, as long as the statutory limitation did not impermissibly intrude on the president’s executive power. Yet the Slaughter Court sees no value in independence and instead insists on unchecked presidential power to remove agency heads.

In National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission, the Court again overturned established precedent for no better reason than the fact that it could. Republicans challenged a long-standing requirement that if political parties coordinate their electoral expenditures with a candidate, they are subject to the strict limits imposed on contributions to candidates. In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the Court held that Congress can limit contributions to candidates but not independent expenditures on their behalf. It reasoned that contributions pose a threat of bribery, or “quid pro quo” corruption, whereas expenditures, if truly independent of the candidate, do not. But the statute subjected “coordinated expenditures” to the same limits as contributions. In Federal Election Commission v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Commission (2001), the Court upheld that rule as applied to expenditures by political parties, deeming it appropriate to avoid circumvention of contribution limits. There is, after all, little distinction between expenditures coordinated with a candidate and direct contributions to that candidate. If I spend $10,000 on campaign advertising that the candidate and I work on together and he approves, that’s effectively the same as giving him $10,000 to spend on his own advertising.

In the NRSC decision, however, the Court reversed its earlier decision and held that Congress cannot restrict parties from coordinating their expenditures with candidates. As Kagan explained in dissent, the practical effect is to invite circumvention of contribution limits; while donors were previously limited to giving $7,000 per election cycle to a candidate, they can now donate more than half a million dollars to a political party for spending coordinated with that candidate. At a time when campaigns are increasingly dominated by the outsize spending of a small number of billionaires, the decision is certain to exacerbate the deeply corrosive influence of money on politics.

The Court’s decision upholding state bans on transgender girls and women playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams, West Virginia v. B.P.J., did not overturn precedent; it simply declined to follow it. The Court concluded that states can exclude trans women from women’s teams because of general physical differences between men and women. The plaintiffs did not challenge the basic division of sports teams into men’s and women’s teams or even the exclusion of most trans women. They argued only that when a trans woman has used puberty blockers and hormone therapy to eliminate any sex-based advantage she might otherwise have from being born male, the state’s interests do not justify the exclusion. Sex discrimination precedent provides that states can draw distinctions based on sex only when they are closely tied to an important government interest. The plaintiffs conceded that the states had important interests in fair competition and safety but argued that those interests were not implicated by trans athletes who had eliminated any sex-based advantage.

In past cases, the Court has held that when a particular group of men or women does not fit the generalization about men and women that is claimed to justify a sex-based rule, the rule is unconstitutional with regard to that group. But as Sotomayor persuasively argued in dissent, the majority failed to require the state to show that trans women who did not undergo puberty and were taking hormone blockers nonetheless posed any threat to either fair competition or safety. Absent such a showing, precedent required that the exclusion be struck down. Yet the majority required no showing and essentially just took the state’s word for it.

The Court also enabled Trump’s cruel anti-immigration policy in two more 6–3 decisions. In Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, it ruled that immigration authorities can turn away asylum seekers at the border without considering whether they face persecution and are therefore eligible for asylum. An immigration statute requires Customs and Border Patrol agents to consider an asylum application from anyone “arriving in” the United States, but the majority ruled that someone stopped at the border has not arrived “in” the country. That decision will permit Trump to turn away people with urgent and valid asylum claims simply by not letting them step foot in the US.

In Mullin v. Doe, the Court held that decisions to eliminate “temporary protected status” (TPS), which is granted to nationals of particular countries where conditions are unsafe for their return, are unreviewable by courts, even if the administration violates the procedures Congress requires for such decisions. The Court expansively interpreted an immigration statute barring judicial review of the DHS secretary’s “determination” on TPS as barring review not just of the ultimate decision but of all steps preceding that determination. The Court’s opinion has the effect of foreclosing any statutory challenge to Trump’s termination of TPS for more than one million foreign nationals.

Even more disturbing was the Court’s rejection, in the Doe case, of a constitutional challenge to the lifting of TPS status for Haitians. The plaintiffs alleged that this decision violated equal protection because Trump had made clear in multiple public statements that it was motivated by race. As Kagan noted in dissent, Trump’s racist statements about Haitians were so distasteful that the majority could not even bring itself to quote them in its opinion. But in dissent Kagan did:

Haitians are “eating the dogs…. They’re eating the cats. They’re eating—they’re eating the pets of the people that live [in Springfield, Ohio].”… And: Haitians are also eating “other things too that they’re not supposed to be.”… And: Haitians in the United States “probably have AIDS.”… And: Haiti is a “shithole country,” which is “filthy, dirty, [and] disgusting.”… And: Haitian immigration is “like a death wish for our country.”… And: Haitians, along with some others, are “poisoning the blood” of our country…. And: “Why is it we only take people from shithole countries” like “Haiti [and] Somalia”? “Why cannot we have some people from Norway [and] Sweden?”

The majority, so offended by any consideration of race for the purpose of affirmative action, blithely asserted that none of these outrageous remarks was “overtly” racist. And as if it somehow makes the racism acceptable, the majority cited a possible nonracial motive for the action—Trump’s general antipathy toward immigrants. There’s little doubt that Trump is a xenophobe as well as a racist, but that is no defense. Equal protection precedents do not require a plaintiff to show that race was the sole motive for a challenged decision, only that it was “a motivating factor.” When one compares Trump’s treatment of Haitians with that of white South Africans, the truth could hardly be more self-evident. Yet much as it did in upholding Trump’s Muslim ban during his first term despite his many expressions of anti-Muslim animus, the majority looked the other way.

The Court’s acceptance of Trump’s racism in the TPS case is all the more galling in light of its ruling in Louisiana v. Callais. In that case, the Court effectively rewrote the Voting Rights Act to render it all but impossible for minority voters to challenge electoral maps that deprive them of a meaningful chance to elect representatives of their choice.3 The Court effectively required proof that a legislature intentionally drew its map to disenfranchise minority voters, even though Congress in 1982 specifically amended the statute to reject a similar judicial interpretation. In that amendment, Congress made clear that minority voters need only show a racially discriminatory effect, not a racially discriminatory motive. The difference is critical because it is often easy to hide racial motives, and Congress’s concern was with objective results, not subjective purposes.

The Court’s conservatives, however, dislike such “effects” tests, because as a practical matter a state may need to consider race to avoid an impermissible discriminatory result, and the conservatives are ideologically committed to colorblindness. But the justices’ ideological preferences don’t justify rewriting a statute to mean exactly what Congress long ago said it does not mean. And when coupled with the TPS decision, it appears that the conservatives are more sensitive to the mere possibility that race might be used to redress the historic underrepresentation of minorities than to its actual use to deny protection to more than 300,000 Haitian immigrants.

In sum, the term just concluded offered good news and bad news. The good news is that the Court will sometimes check Trump when he acts unlawfully. In this sense, it functioned as a court, not as a politically partisan institution. That is essential to the preservation of the rule of law, and should not be discounted.

But the bad news is that the Court is also more willing than ever to thrust aside prior decisions that get in the way of its desired outcomes. Limits on presidential power are essential to a constitutional democracy, but so, too, are limits on the Court’s power. The obligation to follow precedent is the principal check on the judiciary. But the conservative majority seems more willing to constrain Trump than to accept this crucial limit on its own authority.
